author: Jian Zharese Joies Sanz
title: Despite opposition, university admin allows state-sponsored red-tagging forum
content:
The real threat comes from state policies and operations by the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) that silence ordinary citizens.


MANILA — The attacks on youth activists persist following a military-led seminar titled “Community Anti-Terrorism Awareness and Knowing the Enemy” held on July 2 at the Philippine Normal University North Luzon (PNU-NL).


According to The Torch-North Luzonian

news article

, the official student publication of PNU-NL, the seminar was attended by first year to third year students, and featured police officers from 205th Maneuver Company, Regional Mobile Force Battalion 2 (RMFB2) as resource speakers.


In one part of the lecture, the speaker showed photos of alleged dead members of the New People’s Army (NPA) and remarked, “Maybe you guys thought that’s a lechon.”


One of the speakers claimed that universities like the Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP), University of Santo Tomas (UST), and University of the Philippines (UP) are breeding grounds for “rebels”. The speaker added that most rebels come from these universities due to the progressive, idealistic, and excellent nature of their students.


The report by the Torch-North Luzonian said that PNU-NL Executive Director and Provost Agnes S. Reyes initiated and requested the seminar. When asked by the campus publication on the purpose of the seminar in an interview, Dr. Julievic Palting, head of the Student Affairs and Services Unit, said that the seminar was organized to promote civic awareness and help students become more conscious of their actions as citizens.


The seminar was condemned not only by student-attendees but also by progressive youth groups.

Anakbayan–PNU

 said that by cutting off the open forum and shutting down questions from students during the forum, the organizers proved their ulterior motive.


Anakbayan-PNU stressed that the seminar does not promote education as it aims to control the youth’s critical thinking and maintain a culture of violence and impunity. “It is deeply ironic and hypocritical that the very administrators who ought to protect the safety, academic freedom, and welfare of students are the ones orchestrating and opening the door to the militarization of the university. “


More cases


On June 19, state forces red-tagged progressive youth, students, and human rights defenders’ organizations in Barangay 4, Lucban, Quezon Province 


A military personnel shows a presentation about the involvement of youth in progressive organizations during an anti-insurgency forum in Lucban, Quezon, on June 19, 2026. Photo from Kabataan Partylist – Quezon Province


According to

 Kabataan Partylist (KPL)–Quezon

, the forum was used as a front for “anti-insurgency”. The group warned that such state-sponsored labeling puts the lives and security of student leaders at risk.


In a statement, KPL–Quezon denounced the continuous profiling, surveillance, threats, and forced seminars conducted by the military and its intelligence units. They said that these are direct assaults on the youth’s constitutional rights to free expression, organization, and social participation.


The group questioned the entry of Southern Luzon Command (SOLCOM) into academic institutions. “The continuous collaboration and opening up of universities to military units or the SOLCOM is highly questionable, especially when it results in the entry of programs that promote red-tagging and intimidate students. Universities must remain safe spaces for free expression, critical study, and democratic participation—not battlegrounds for military operations and counter-insurgency propaganda.”


On May 31, the student alliance

 Rise for Education–SLSU (Southern Luzon State University) reported

 that state agents are gathering personal information of students who advocate for democratic rights.


Aside from profiling, the student alliance said that activists have been receiving threatening messages from suspected state-backed online trolls. Meanwhile, the military’s community-level “anti-insurgency” seminars continue to feature discussions that label legal mass organizations as terrorist fronts, generating widespread fear among youth and residents.


Supreme Court ruling and demilitarization


Red-tagging persists despite a landmark

 Supreme Court ruling in May 2024

 which declared that red-tagging, vilification, labeling, and guilt by association constitute threats to a person’s right to life …

author: groundxero
title: The Saudi–Turkish–Pakistani Security Agreement: A preliminary assessment
content:
The signing of a security and defence agreement by three countries allied with the United States cannot be viewed lightly, since it may stir significant strategic shifts in the Middle East.


 


by

Dr Sania Faisal El-Husseini


 


The Mecca Agreement, signed on 7 August, may not be the first step in a series of moves that key states in the region have begun to take, reflecting significant strategic shifts.


 


Although the challenges facing the countries of the region are not new, they have intensified markedly in recent years. The Israeli wars on Gaza, and its expansion into the US-Israeli war on Iran during the current presidency of Donald Trump, have undoubtedly provided the most significant impetus for countries in the region to reconsider their external strategic calculations, their roles, and their standing within the region.


 


The collective security and deterrence nature of the agreement between these states carries a particular significance and represents an important development in regional security equations and deterrence strategies, in a region where the United States has long worked to establish a different set of arrangements. The agreement can be regarded as a particular message to the United States, especially as it calls on other influential states to join it, foremost among them Egypt and Qatar. These countries share a number of characteristics relating to their standing, their military and security systems, the threats surrounding them, and the regional alliances arrayed against them, which help to explain the importance of their alliance, its purpose, the reasons for their concerns, and their efforts to protect themselves.


 


The challenge, however, remains in implementing the agreement, which depends on establishing a mechanism for activating its collective security clause namely, treating an attack on one member of the alliance as an attack on all the others. The question, then, is whether the agreement can succeed in the complex and consequential task of establishing new realities that must be taken into account in the region’s balance of power, whose relative weights have long been determined by the United States alone.


 


The weight and standing of the three countries involved in the Mecca Agreement may be the most important reason it has attracted attention. The agreement brings together Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. Saudi Arabia holds considerable economic and political weight in the region, while Turkey combines a significant geopolitical presence with promising and rapidly advancing military-industrial expertise; it has the second-largest military in NATO after the United States. Pakistan, meanwhile, is the only nuclear power among the Arab and Muslim countries of the region and has extensive combat experience shaped by a conflict that has lasted for decades. Saudi Arabia and Turkey also share an affiliation with the Western military tradition: the former has relied for decades on the American defence establishment, while the latter is one of NATO’s key members and is firmly rooted in the Western military tradition. All three countries are allies of the United States, albeit to varying degrees. They also share an evolving approach to their domestic defence strategies, although the timing and pace of that development have differed among them. Pakistan has sought to diversify its sources of external military dependence. Having relied strongly on the United States during the Cold War, it has now become a major partner of China, which has surpassed the United States in this respect. Turkey, by contrast, remains a member of NATO while also operating elements of a Russian defence system, an approach it adopted nearly a decade ago. Today, it has developed an independent military profile over recent decades alongside its NATO commitments.


 


Saudi Arabia, for its part, has for years been developing a strategy based on greater self-reliance in manufacturing, including in the military sector. It has also begun diversifying the sources of its military arsenal after previously relying almost entirely on the United States.


 


Today, all three countries are seeking greater independence in security decision-making, arms procurement and even their alliances, a development that represents a genuine shift and a challenge for the United States.


 


The early signs of efforts to build this kind of collective defence arrangement in the region could already be seen last year …

author: rti_admin
title: We Are Not Your Little Anything: On the Portrayal of Mizoram and the Ethics of Being Seen
content:
You scroll through a reel of Aizawl at dusk. The camera pans across the ridge. Terraced houses cling to the slope, holding on the way our houses do because our land is nearly vertical and there is nowhere else for them to sit. The light is soft. The audio is Japanese, likely a scrap of dialogue pulled from a series or a film and laid over the frame. It is not translating anything; it has no connection to what you are looking at. It is there because it sounds like somewhere else, and that is what aesthetic means now.

I have been thinking about that reel for weeks and about the comments under it. Most of them are from Mizos. Most are proud – feels like Kyoto, little Japan of India, hard to believe this is India. And I have been trying to name precisely what is wrong with the fact that we are the ones cheering.

A recent essay on this platform traced how counterculture and marginalized aesthetics only become palatable once dominant groups appropriate, sanitize or rebrand them. That essay was writing about punk, about Gandhi’s ascetic performance, about the Mary Kom yellowface. I want to extend the argument in a direction the writer only gestures toward – what happens when the aesthetic being consumed is not a jacket or a film but a land, a festival, a woman in puan (traditional Mizo wrap) at Chapchar Kut and the consumers arrive by the trainload.

The friend who stopped being interesting

A friend told me a story recently. She was at her hostel in a mainland university, and a non-Northeast girl came up to her, bright and curious, and asked where she was from. Meghalaya, my friend said. The girl became warm, generous, full of questions. They chatted for a while. Then at dinner, in a group, someone mentioned in passing that Meghalaya is a state in India, the girl went quiet. She stopped speaking to my friend. Over the course of the evening she drifted away, and by the next day she had forgotten my friend existed.

I keep returning to that story because it captures the machinery so cleanly. My friend was interesting when she was foreign. She became invisible the moment she was recategorized as Indian. Nothing about her had changed. What changed was the girl’s calculation of what my friend was worth to her – as an exotic acquaintance, potentially high; as a fellow citizen from a place she considered peripheral, nothing. That transaction is what governs how mainland India encounters the Northeast now and it is what governs the shape of the tourism arriving in Mizoram.

Little Switzerland, Little Japan, Little Anywhere-But-Here

The comparisons come constantly. Little Switzerland. Little Japan. Just like Korea. The whole vocabulary is diminutive. Not Switzerland. Little Switzerland. The mainland viewer is not permitted to see Mizoram as itself. They can only see it as a pocket substitute for somewhere they would rather be, somewhere they cannot afford to fly to. The land is granted value only through comparison and only as a smaller, cheaper, more accessible version of an actual destination.

What this does is protect the viewer from having to revise their mental map. Mizoram is allowed to be beautiful only if that beauty is imported. The moment the beauty is claimed as Indian and Mizo, on its own terms, the frame collapses. That is why you see the second move so often – the pivot to “see, this is India too, not a foreign land.” When someone points out that Aizawl does not honk, that Mizos queue, that the streets are clean, the same voice that a moment ago called it Little Switzerland now insists that this is India, this is us. Both moves are doing the same work. Both are refusing to let Mizoram be Indian and orderly at the same time, because that would force a reckoning with why the places the viewer considers the real India are neither.

The railway reaching Aizawl has been described in the national press as a milestone of connectivity. It is. It is also a distribution system for this gaze at scale. When I first heard the trains were coming, my thought was not about goods or jobs. It was about the tourists. How were we going to handle them, not in the logistical sense. In the sense of what they would do when they arrived believing they had earned access to a curiosity and what we would feel obliged to give them.

At festivals across the Northeast now, videos are circulating of men, tourists from the mainland, grabbing women in traditional attire to pose for photographs. Sometimes the woman is pulled by the arm. Sometimes …

author: Mekong Review 2
title: The cost of visibility Nathalie Chi
content:
Protests against the Chinese mega-embassy in London. Credit: Monkey Butler Images F ace covered, recognisable features hidden. A back-up phone in hand, location services disabled. No recent travel plans. No recent contact with family members in Tibet. Avoid cameras. Avoid interviews. At political protests against the Chinese government, including recent demonstrations against the planned Chinese mega-embassy in London, some Tibetan participants arrive with these calculations already made. Not everyone takes the same precautions, but everyone understands the necessity. Visibility travels, particularly for Tibetans. A single photograph, name, or online post can instantly cross borders, reaching far beyond the crowd standing on a London street. This landscape of fear has recently gained a physical anchor. In January 2026, the UK government approved China’s plan to redevelop the Royal Mint Court in central London into its largest diplomatic mission in Europe. The plan has faced sustained opposition from local residents, campaign groups, and politicians, who have raised concerns over national security, surveillance, protest safety, and the impact on surrounding areas. author: Benjamin Cordero
title: Ang Paglalayag sa Kawalan: Isang Pagsusuri sa The Odyssey (2026)
content:
Isang dambuhalang tagumpay sa sining ng pelikula ang The Odyssey (2026) ni Christopher Nolan. Bagaman napakamahal na ng halaga ng sine sa kasalukuyang panahon, isa itong biswal na hiyas na nararapat panoorin sa pinakamalaking telon hangga’t maaari. Ngunit sa ilalim ng nagngangalit na alon ng Dagat Mediteranyo o sa sindak na dulot ng Cyclops o sa bigat ng modernong pagganap na dala ni Matt Damon, may kuwentong pumipintig sa isang napakapamilyar na paraan.

Ang panonood ng The Odyssey sa pamamagitan ng matang Pilipino ay parang nakararanas ng matinding déjà vu . Para sa isang kulturang hinubog ng pangingibang-bansa, walang-katapusang pagtitiis, at pagkakawatak-watak ng pamilya, ang sampung taong pakikipagsapalaran ni Odysseus para lang makauwi ay hindi lang kuwento ng mitolohiyang Griyego—ito mismo ang buhay at kalagayan ng modernong Pilipino.

Ang pinakamabilis at pinakamatinding koneksyon ng pelikula ni Nolan sa buhay-Pilipino ay ang karakter mismo ni Odysseus. Siya ay isang lalaking nakakulong sa isang walang-awa at nakapapagod na pagpapatapon sa sarili. Sa pelikula, mariing ipinakita ni Nolan ang sikolohikal na epekto ng pagkakahiwalay ni Odysseus sa kanyang bayan; hindi lang siya lumalaban sa mga halimaw, kundi lumalaban din siya sa oras, sa distansya, at sa unti-unting paglaho ng alaala ng tahanang kanyang iniwan.

Ito ang salamin ng totoong buhay ng milyun-milyong Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), ang ating mga bagong bayani. Katulad ni Odysseus na umalis ng Ithaca para lumaban sa digmaan sa Troy para sa kanyang bayan, ang OFW ay umaalis din sa Pilipinas para lumaban sa isang digmaang pang-ekonomiko sa dayuhang lupain. Pareho silang ginagabayan ng iisang layunin: ang buhayin, protektahan, at sa huli ay balikan ang pamilyang kanilang minamahal.

Kapag nakatulala si Odysseus (Matt Damon) sa karagatan habang nakakulong sa isla ng Ogygia, sinumang Pilipinong nanonood ay makikita ang mukha ng ating mga tita, tito, ina, at ama na nagpupuyat habang nakatingin sa bintana ng mga matataas na gusali sa Hong Kong, Dubai, o Singapore. Ang mga halimaw na hinarap ni Odysseus—ang mapanlinlang na akit ni Circe o ang nakaparalisang pagkalimot na dala ng mga Lotus-Eater—ay madaling maitumbas sa mga panganib ng pangingibang-bansa ngayon: (1) Ang tuksong makiangkop nang tuluyan sa dayuhang kultura at limutin ang sariling pinagmulan. (2) Ang mabigat at mapag-isang depresyon ng pagiging dayuhan sa ibang bansa at; (3) Ang mga burukrasya, kahirapan sa bayang babalikan at pisikal na hadlang na nagpapatagal sa pag-uwi nang maraming taon, o dekada.

Habang nakikipaglaban si Odysseus sa malalaking alon, ang bigat ng emosyon ng pelikula ay pasan naman nina Penelope (Anne Hathaway) at Telemachus (Tom Holland) sa Ithaca. Mahusay na ipinakita ni Nolan na ang Ithaca ay hindi isang marangyang kaharian na naghihintay sa kanilang hari, kundi isang gumuguhong bahay na kinatatawanan ng mga mapagsamantalang manliligaw/dayuhan na unti-unting nagpapasasa sa kanilang yaman.

Ang bahaging ito ng kuwento ay napakasakit tanggapin para sa mga pamilyang Pilipino. Kapag ang isang magulang ay umalis ng Pilipinas para magtrabaho sa abroad, ang pamilyang naiwan ay parang nakabinbin sa hangin. Si Penelope ang sumasalamin sa nakatutunaw at mapag-isang dusa ng asawang naiwan—na kadalasan ay ang ina na mag-isang nagtataguyod sa bahay, nagpoprotekta sa mga anak laban sa mga mapagsamantalang tao sa lipunan, at nagkukunwaring matatag kahit na nadudurog ang puso sa tindi ng pangungulila.

Si Telemachus naman ang kumakatawan sa “anak ng OFW.” Ipinakita ni Tom Holland ang isang binatang puno ng kumplikadong emosyon—may galit, may pangungulila, at may matinding pressure. Lumaki siya sa ilalim ng anino ng isang tanyag na ama na halos hindi niya matandaan, at napilitang ipagtanggol ang kanilang tahanan bago pa siya maging handa. Sa pang-araw-araw na buhay ng Pilipino, ito ang realidad ng milyun-milyong bata na lumalaki sa pamamagitan lamang ng video calls at remittance slips. Lumalaki silang walang ama o ina sa tabi, napipilitang magmatured nang maaga, nakalantad sa nauusong karahasan (maging sa sariling paaralan) at pasan ang bigat ng sakripisyo ng magulang habang nahihirapan ding kilalanin ang sarili.

Sa kaibuturan nito, ang The Odyssey ay isang paggalugad sa konsepto ng nostos—ang sinaunang salitang Griyego para sa pagbabalik-bayan. Sa kulturang Pilipino, ito ang ating pinakamalalim na mithiin: ang konsepto ng pagbabalik o pag-uwi.

author: Kevin Lin
title: The Seven Deadly Sins of Conferencing
content:
Many of us know from experience that the most memorable and enjoyable parts of participating in a conference are the tea and coffee breaks, the conversations lunches and dinners, the informal chats outside of the conference room while the meeting is still happening, and the late-night hangouts with other participants. Genuinely good conversations take place and relationships are formed or renewed in those moments. So why don’t we recognise what is obvious, and create structures that bring out these experiences?


Social movements rely on purposeful gatherings to connect, share experiences, and strategise. We do this so often we should be really good at it. But more often than not, things do not seem to quite work. This has prompted me to reflect, and then test my impressions with other conference-goers who turn out to be feeling much the same ways. I need to first acknowledge how much unseen labour goes into any event planning; the event organisers are the most invisible if everything goes well. But it is necessary to recognise and name things that do not seem to work.


Here are the seven deadly sins of conference organising. I want to speak to my fellow conference organisers: of course, not all of us committed all of the sins, and some of you have done much better. But many of the sins would sound familiar to us, and we often let our guards down. By naming them, we may do a better job at avoiding them, and get to organise and experience more effective, creative and joyful gatherings.


 


Greed


 


The first sin is greed. We are often greedy about what can be accomplished with a gathering, especially with sizable conferences. We want to invite many people to be there to meet and connect, while also want them to have substantial discussions.


A medium to large conference of dozens to a few hundred people is amazing. But it is not primarily a place for deep learning or for substantial conversations despite our best efforts and most sincere wishes. There are simply too many sessions, too many speakers and too many people to learn and engage deeply. We listen to one panel after another and hardly remember anything from each speaker, while facilitators apologise for running out of time and no more time for questions. We then try to have conversations during breaks that on average last for 5 to 10 minutes before rushing back to the next session or talking or introducing ourselves to someone else. You should not feel alone in experiencing this.


We know deep learning and substantial conversation are most likely to take place in much smaller meetings. You may really have to keep it to a very small number of participants, arguably no more than 10 or 15 but maybe even fewer, to have sustained conversations that give everyone time to think, allow ideas to develop, and for them to build on each other’s ideas.


The medium and large conferences serve other important goals: it is good for building new relationships or renewing old ones, for feeling part of a larger movement with many others with shared values and goals, and for experiencing the optimism and joy of movement-building. It is good enough to take away with you the connections you have made, a sense of the movement’s diversity and creativity, and the fact that people are doing the best they can under enormous pressure and risk.


If these are the realistic goals, then our task is to structure the events in ways that let people and ideas to breath, to have both structured discussions and unstructured time for spontaneous conversations, and to make these events into festivals.


 


Busyness


 


The second sin is busyness. Far too often, I have been in conference planning where the logistics – the venue search and booking, the travel arrangement, the drinks, snacks and meals, and the interpretation – take up most of the planning time. We end up spending very little time discussing and experimenting with the actual program. In fact, the program design at times feels like an afterthought.


The logistics discussions and preparations are often not completely done until the very last minute. Time for a program discussion tends to be squeezed in between logistics discussions. When we are tight on time, we tend to revert to the familiar and the safest: let us get these speakers speakers for these panels, and each speaks for 15 minutes. It is the least that can go wrong. No one can claim they love this, but we keep doing it anyway.


It may be worth aiming to reserve a …

author: Rojava IC
title: Sleeper-Cell Report June 2026 – Justice Palace Department’s Head Killed
content:
The head of the Palace of Justice was seriously injured after being targeted in an attack on June 16. 


 


Key Points 


Five sleeper cell attacks were recorded in June; a slight increase from only three in May


A total of four military personnel were killed, and at least two injured 


Fatalities of two suspected ISIS affiliates were also recorded


Paper leaflets containing Pro-ISIS propaganda were distributed in several provinces throughout Syria


 


In Depth


This month, RIC recorded a total five attacks, two of which have been directly claimed by ISIS at the time of writing, the remaining three are believed to have been carried out by ISIS members.


On June 15, unidentified gunmen believed to be of an ISIS cell attacked the headquarters of general security forces, two of its members were killed and several others injured, west of Raqqa city, before one of the attackers self-detonated.  


On June 16, Salah Ahmad al-Saleh, head of the Palace of Justice in the town of Babila in rural Damascus was seriously injured by an explosive device attached to his vehicle. And on the same day, ISIS members targeted an oil tanker with machine-gun fire near the northern city of Manbij. Material damage to the tanker was reported.


On June 20, unidentified gunmen believed to be part of an ISIS cell, attacked members of the 76th Armored Division, causing the death of two Division’s members. The attack occurred near Tahnah junction in the western countryside of Manbij.


On June 24, two gunmen believed to be ISIS members, on a motorcycle opened fire on two members of the Engineering Regiment of the 72nd Division, on Ain Issa Road in Raqqa countryside, injuring both of them. 


On June 19, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces conducted an airstrike in northwest Syria. CENTCOM confirmed the killing of Ali Husayn al-‘Ulaywi, a senior ISIS leader. 


Paper leaflets were distributed in several mosques across different areas in Daraa, Idlib and Aleppo provinces. The leaflets contain extremist content and rhetoric linked to ISIS.


Save the Children, an Australian children’s advocacy organization, called for the return of an ISIS-linked Australian woman and her disabled child from Syria after a failed repatriation attempt. Following the failed departure, Syrian authorities reportedly transferred them to a detention facility in northwestern Syria’s Idlib Governorate, since then, her family lost contact with her.


Another Australian woman was accused of supporting ISIS and appeared before a court in Melbourne, where prosecutors alleged she lived in a household that held a teenage girl in slavery while the victim was subjected to repeated abuse.  Her request for bail was rejected, as prosecutors argued she poses a risk to public safety. 


Tammy Bruce, U.S. Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ambassador said that it would continue working with Syria to combat ISIS, and support efforts to preserve stability and safety in the country.

title: Fire at camp housing displaced people from Shengal: 10 tents destroyed
content:
A fire broke out around midday at Shariya Camp in Duhok, where displaced people from Shengal are staying. The fire, which reportedly started after a gas cylinder exploded, completely destroyed 10 tents.


Pîrdiyan Cefer, an official with the Duhok Directorate of Migration and Refugee Affairs, said that no one was injured in the fire, but that extensive material damage had occurred.


Cefer said that Civil Defense and firefighting teams managed to bring the fire under control within a short time, adding that an investigation into the incident had been launched.


Emergency relief efforts have also been initiated for the families whose tents were destroyed.

author: James McVicar
title: Students teach Hanson a lesson
content:
Across the country yesterday, students walked out of their schoolrooms and lecture halls and flooded into the streets to protest against Pauline Hanson and her far-right political project.

As many as 4,000 marched in Sydney. Two thousand in Perth and Adelaide and 1,000 in Brisbane. In Canberra, 500 students protested at the Australian National University campus and 200 turned out in Wollongong. High schoolers spontaneously organised protests in Shoalhaven, Lismore, and Albury. In Melbourne, where I was, the march was colossal—about 5,000 people—and the mood was absolutely electric.

The chants rang out with righteous rage: “Too young to protest? We call bullshit!” and “High school, uni, teachers too; Pauline Hanson, we’re coming for you!” Undoubtedly the most popular was a two-word refrain: “Fuck Pauline!” Sometimes less is more.

The homemade placards were funny and indignant and withering. “I love naps but I stay woke”. “Still got a better attendance rate than Hanson”. “Orange is the new evil”. On the ground I spotted a papier-mache Hanson head that, from the looks of it, had had a run-in with a few too many shiny black shoes.

Anyone over the age of 25 knows what it’s like to be roasted by teenagers. Gen Z sarcasm is one of the most devastating weapons humankind has ever known. So just try to imagine how Hanson must be feeling right now.

All she could muster as a response was a post on X: “If you want to protest something, protest why your parents’ wages are going backwards and the cost of everything is going up ... Whether you know it or not, One Nation and I are fighting for you”. Please don’t hurt me, kids, I’m actually on your side! Pathetic.

The students were protesting against the increasing entrenchment of far-right politics in Australia being spearheaded by Hanson and One Nation. It’s clear to them that Hanson’s reactionary agenda only serves the big end of town. It’s not just Gina Rinehart: more and more wealthy backers are swinging in behind One Nation.

Hanson’s project to demonise migrants and attack the rights of women and workers helps to prop up a society where the few rule over the many. Odessa, a High School Anti-Capitalists member from Huntingtower, hit the nail on the head in her speech: “We know she’s a servant for the wealthy”.

At the same time, the mainstream parties have ceded more and more ground to One Nation. The Liberals are doing their level best to rebrand as One Nation in neckties. Labor politicians are planning to announce substantial cuts to migration. They too want to run a system based on extreme wealth inequality, hard borders and minority rule, so we cannot count on them to stand up to the far right.

One Nation’s rise is part of a broader global shift in politics. Aero, an international student at RMIT and member of Socialist Alternative, spoke about President Javier Milei in Argentina, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Italy, Nigel Farage in the UK and Donald Trump in America. Students know what’s going on abroad and know it needs to be fought. “Australia does not need our own orange clown”, read one placard.

Around the world, capitalism has less and less to offer people but wage cuts and declining living standards. As governments pour more and more money into war preparations, welfare and social spending are being slashed. The far-right’s authoritarian politics, their championing of social hierarchy and oppression—it all fits the bill for our rulers.

In the middle of the State Library forecourt, the haughty statue of Supreme Court judge and first chancellor of Melbourne University Redmond Barry became a rostrum for unruly teens calling out “Pauline Hanson is a fascist!” Old Redmond would have had a fit. The other two statues outside the State Library—St George slaying a dragon on one side and a triumphant Joan of Arc on the other—seemed a little more the vibe of the day.

This was a protest of students from schools and universities across the country, but the high schoolers were the heroes of the day. I spoke to students from Melbourne High who reckoned there were 40 of them marching. Another 50 from both Northcote High and Coburg High. There were thousands more, including students from as far away as Geelong, Ballarat and Bendigo. Sixty schools were represented at the Sydney rally. In Perth, rally organisers say students from 120 different schools contacted them about joining the strike.

Plenty of high schoolers had to fight for their right to even be there in the …

author: Carissa Lee
title: MEDIA STATEMENT : FELIPE ALVAREZ CORONIAL INQUEST
content:
FELIPE ALVAREZ: FAMILY CALLS FOR ACCOUNTABILITY, TRANSPARENCY AND CORONIAL REFORM AFTER ACT CORONER’S FINDINGS


By Gabriela Alvarez-Sledge

Sister of the late Felipe Esteban Alvarez


Disclaimer: Readers please be advised this article mentions someone who has passed away.


“Felipe’s life mattered. His death mattered. What we learn from his death matters.”


The family of the late

Felipe Esteban Alvarez

 is calling for greater transparency, accountability and reform of the ACT coronial system following the release of the findings into his death.


Felipe died in March 2021 following an overdose at his Canberra residence.


Five years later, his family is still grieving while asking an important question:


What can be changed so that another family does not have to go through what ours has experienced?


Felipe was not simply a coronial file.


He was a brother, son, uncle and deeply loved member of his family.


His life had value.


His family believes his death deserved to be investigated as thoroughly, transparently and independently as possible.


WHAT THE CORONER FOUND


The findings of ACT Coroner Ken Archer identified serious concerns surrounding the circumstances of Felipe’s death.


The Coroner found that Felipe was experiencing a medical emergency and that emergency medical assistance was not sought for a significant period of time.


The Coroner found that the delay deprived Felipe of any chance of survival he may have had following his initial collapse.


The Coroner described the conduct of those present as

“morally blameworthy”

 and found that their conduct demonstrated a serious indifference to the possibility of loss of life.


The findings also identified broader public-safety concerns relating to the Canberra Alliance for Harm Minimisation and Advocacy (CAHMA), including concerns about governance, recruitment and screening, overdose-response training, naloxone availability and organisational accountability.


The Coroner found that appropriate screening and eligibility processes should have been applied to the relevant peer workers.


The findings also raised concerns about the organisation’s response following Felipe’s death and the need for stronger governance and accountability.


The Coroner recommended improvements to overdose-response training and stronger collaboration between harm-minimisation services, health agencies, ambulance services and police.


The family welcomes those recommendations.


THE FAMILY’S CONCERNS REMAIN


Throughout the coronial process, Felipe’s family provided information, documents and concerns about matters they believed were important to understanding what happened.


The family identified people who were present when Felipe suffered his overdose and sought to have the relevant evidence properly considered.


The family also provided written material that it believed was relevant to understanding what occurred.


However, the family remained concerned that not every matter it believed was important was fully tested or explored during the coronial process.


Because the Court has imposed restrictions concerning the publication of identities,

the family will not identify any person whose identity is subject to suppression

.


The family respects the Court’s orders.


There will be no naming of suppressed individuals in this statement.


The family’s concern has never been about publicly naming people.


It is about evidence.


It is about transparency.


It is about whether families can have confidence that every reasonable avenue of inquiry has been considered when their loved one dies.


THIS IS NOT AN ATTACK ON THE CORONER


The family wishes to make this position very clear.


Gabriela   Alvarez-Sledge is not seeking to undermine the independence of the Coroner or interfere with the findings.


She acknowledges the Coroner’s findings and welcomes the public-safety recommendations.


The family’s concern is about what can be learned from the entire experience.


A coronial system should not only determine how a person died.


It should also give bereaved families confidence that the investigation was thorough, transparent, fair and independent.


Where families continue to have genuine concerns about aspects of a coronial process, there should be an appropriate and independent pathway for those concerns to be considered.


A CALL FOR CORONIAL REFORM


Felipe’s sister, Gabriela   Alvarez-Sledge, is calling for the ACT Government to consider meaningful …

author: AWSM
title: A Community in the Cracks of Capitalism
content:
A piece of Christchurch that the property market abandoned after the earthquakes has become home to people abandoned by the property market. The old Bexley neighbourhood was largely cleared after liquefaction made conventional residential development impossible. Houses disappeared, streets remained and the land sat waiting for whatever official purpose would eventually be found for it. Into that gap came people who needed somewhere to live. They arrived in cars, vans, buses and tents. Some were working. Some were retired. Some had children. They did what people have always done when the institutions around them fail, they improvised. A community grew. Earlier this year about 40 people were living around Wetlands Grove; reports now put the number at more than 100. Christchurch City Council has told them they must leave by 28 February 2027 because the area is intended for wetland development. There is an obvious temptation to treat this as a story about homelessness, council planning or the difficulties of finding somewhere suitable for a group of people living in vehicles. It is all of those things, but underneath them sits a much simpler question. What is land for? The answer given by our economic system is that land belongs to whoever has legal title to it, and its legitimate use is determined by owners, planners and institutions. The people actually living on it remain secondary. They may sleep there, look after one another there and make the place usable through their own effort, but none of that gives them any meaningful claim to it. Their relationship to the place exists only for as long as the legal owner tolerates it. That distinction between ownership and use lies close to the heart of the anarchist criticism of private property.

The people living at Wetlands Grove have already demonstrated something that governments spend enormous amounts of money trying unsuccessfully to manufacture through policy documents – people can organise social life themselves. Earlier reporting described an informal community growing around buses, vans and cars, with neighbours helping one another through winter and a communal tent being established as shared space. One man who had been sleeping in a small tent was helped into an old car when the cold became severe. Council rubbish collection and portable toilets made conditions more bearable, but the social organisation of the place came largely from the people living there. Moko, one of the informal figures in the community, was working full-time on an on-call road crew. Others were pensioners. Ngawai Timu described abandoning a $470-a-week rental because she felt she was spending her life paying somebody else’s mortgage. Polly Stewart was surviving on the pension in a bus. Families were living there too, including a woman with several children living from a bus. These details matter because homelessness is constantly spoken about as though it were primarily a pathology of homeless people. Addiction, mental illness, poor budgeting, antisocial behaviour and bad choices are summoned as explanations because those explanations leave the social order intact. They allow us to imagine that housed people possess some quality that homeless people lack. Wetlands Grove makes that story harder to sustain. When people with jobs cannot obtain housing, when pensioners decide rent leaves too little for ordinary life, and when families find themselves competing with dozens of others for a private rental, the problem is no longer plausibly located inside the individual. There are certainly people living rough who struggle with addiction or serious psychological distress. There are also people who get up and go to work from a tent. A housing system that cannot reliably house either has failed at the most elementary level.

New Zealand has become remarkably skilled at describing this failure without challenging the institution producing it. We talk about housing supply, affordability pressures and housing need. We devise eligibility categories and waiting lists. We construct administrative pathways through emergency housing, transitional housing, community housing and social housing. Every stage acquires its own assessments and rules. The language becomes more sophisticated while people remain without homes. At the 2023 Census, Statistics New Zealand estimated that at least 112,496 people were experiencing severe housing deprivation, around 2.3 percent of the usually resident population. The …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Stand with RAFFWU, oppose Vic Labor’s ‘anti-association’ bill
content:
The Victorian Labor government, under its new Premier Ben Carroll, announced plans on August 12 to introduce a new law to close down unions that have registered as incorporated associations.

The Associations Incorporation Reform Amendment Bill 2026 would affect the Retail and Fast Food Workers Union (RAFFWU), which was forced to register as an incorporated association in Victoria because of the discriminatory federal system.

This archaic system prevents a new union, like RAFFWU, from registering if there is already a union covering a particular industry — in this case, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Union (SDA).

RAFFWU would have registered if not for these undemocratic restrictions, which, in this case, force workers to remain in a do-nothing union like the SDA.

Labor claims the law is needed because “red unions register as ordinary community associations instead of real unions”. “Red unions” do not organise workers to fight for their rights; they market themselves as “alternatives” to traditional unions registering as unincorporated associations. They are right wing and actively oppose COVID-19 measures, including vaccine mandates.

However, the only red unions registered as unincorporated associations are in Toowoomba, Queensland. This means that Carroll’s bill is a thinly veiled attempt to close down an effective union — RAFFWU.

RAFFWU, established 10 years ago, is a grassroots member-led union. It was formed after Fair Work Commission (FWC) hearings in 2015 overturned enterprise bargaining agreements (EBAs) between Coles, McDonald’s, Domino’s Pizza, IGA, Bakers Delight and other major employers, and the SDA.

In each case, the EBAs were overturned because they were found to have left workers worse off than they would have been under the relevant award.

The FWC hearings were instigated by retail and fast-food workers. Since its founding, RAFFWU has gone from strength to strength, organising in more workplaces and winning real gains for workers.

RAFFWU secured a win at Dominos, when the Federal Court of Australia ruled in July in favour of thousands of delivery drivers and instore workers in a class action. The court found that Domino’s had engaged in “misleading or deceptive conduct” by instructing its Australian franchisees to pay staff under a 2005 enterprise agreement rate, which excluded key entitlements, instead of the higher-paying Fast Food Industry Award.

It estimated the ⁠former workers’ loss at about $8326.10, plus interest, after finding that ​Domino’s caused them ​to ⁠suffer loss through underpayment. Domino’s is considering an appeal.

Josh Cullinan, speaking for RAFFWU on July 26, said: “When members explained how old rotten SDA deals were ripping them off at Domino’s Pizza, we knew something was off.”

Cullinan said the union undertook an investigation in 2018 and found “a system of exploitation perpetrated by a multi-billion-dollar franchiser on some of Australia’s lowest-paid workers”. He said the court “has vindicated our campaign and set the record straight”.

RAFFWU also successfully initiated a class action for a paid 10-minute break for McDonald’s workers in shifts between four and nine hours, and two 10-minute paid breaks for shifts longer than nine hours. The action alleged that McDonald’s operated a system of work that denied McDonald’s workers their right to paid breaks in breach of the enterprise agreement and the award.

RAFFWU’s successful organising of McDonald’s workers meant that they received a 25% casual loading rate in addition to penalty rates; a 25% Saturday loading and 35% Sunday loading rate; weekday morning and evening penalty rates; and free uniforms.

The very existence of RAFFWU, which is run by a team of young people working in the industry and organises workers to win real gains, is a political threat to the SDA.

Labor’s new bill, which it says will “stop hate groups from incorporating” will be welcomed by the corporate bosses at Coles, Woolworths and ALDI, who prefer to make deals with the SDA.

Carroll owes his parliamentary seat and his elevation to premier to the powerful SDA faction in the Labor Party — this bill that would abolish RAFFWU is about repaying the favour.

Outrageously, the Victorian Trades Hall Council (VTHC) never allowed RAFFWU to affiliate and is now cheering on this bill.

Retail and fast-food workers should be allowed to join whichever union they choose, and it is little wonder that they are joining RAFFWU, given it has …

author: Luca Tavan
title: Rebel teachers taking their campaign against the Labor government all the way to parliament
content:
“I’m a rebel teacher running against Ben Carroll in Niddrie because I think workers should run the world. I think teachers know how to run schools, and we should be empowered to run the education system ... On the issue of education, the ALP is not just out of touch: they’re on the other side of the picket line, with the Liberals and One Nation.”

This is how Brendan Laws announced the Victorian “rebel educator” campaign—a group of teachers and education support staff targeting sitting Labor MPs, including Premier and former Minister for Education Ben Carroll. 

The eight candidates, all members of Victorian Socialists and the Socialists in Schools union group, have played a role in leading the rank-and-file rebellion in the Australian Education Union (AEU) Victorian Branch that has organised two massive strike days, stared down the state government and fought tooth and nail against the conservative leadership of their own union. The teachers’ fight is the most significant industrial dispute in Victoria in years, with teachers holding the line for a decent contract in the context of falling real wages and deteriorating working conditions. For many on the left, the obstinacy of Victorian Labor in the face of teachers’ demands for decent pay and tolerable working conditions embodies everything wrong with a government which once boasted of running “the most progressive state in the nation”.

Labor has governed Victoria practically uninterrupted for more than two decades, leaning heavily on the support of union members to win successive elections. AEU members were a central part of the mobilisation of 2,200 unionists who doorknocked and phone-banked to hand Daniel Andrews a surprise victory in 2014. 

Twelve years on, Victoria has the lowest-funded public schools in the country. The government has stolen $16 billion from the system through underfunding in the last seven years alone. Surging workloads, wage suppression and increasing class sizes have created a situation in which less than a third of teachers plan to stay in the sector long-term. 

Leading teacher unionist and Victorian Socialists candidate for Niddrie Brendan Laws says:

“The school I’m working at right now is relatively well resourced, but the sheer amount of work and stress is overwhelming. You’re writing and rewriting assessments, you’re marking, trying to give individual feedback. There’s this pressure, because the school is competing with over-funded private schools ... I was at a very low-income school in Werribee; you could see all the traps that students get pulled into, not having the resources to read and learn, at the same time as [Labor] were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on a nearby youth prison. You would just see the kids that were getting pulled out of school into that constantly. Eight teachers quit from my department during one school year so there weren’t enough staff and everybody else had to pull in just to fill in the gaps.”

The AEU leadership’s close-knit relationship with the Labor government means many educators feel the officials have worked against members’ interests. Workers went backwards after their 2022 contract negotiation, when the AEU leadership rushed through a sell-out deal cutting real wages by 11 percent. Forty percent of AEU members voted against the offer, at the time a historically unprecedented rejection of a leadership decision in the union. While many left the union in disgust, others waited, and pledged that next time around it would be different  

Brendan was one of around a dozen Victorian Socialists members who decided to launch Socialists in Schools in mid-2025. “The biggest indicator that there was an audience for it was how many AEU members were already part of Victorian Socialists”, he says. “We took a survey and found we had almost 100 teacher members, so it just showed that there was already a base to work with.” 

The campaign started with the modest aim of giving socialist teachers a chance to get together and chat:

“The first part was just meeting up and discussing socialist politics with the people in our campaign. It was the political arguments around militarism, the genocide in Palestine, the Labor government’s austerity and privatisation. Then when we knew that our last agreement was going to expire and the opportunity to have industrial action was going to be there, we really shifted a lot of our propaganda to educate people about striking. It had been 13 years since a strike had …

author: Sheree Lowe
title: Our Children are the Treaty generation
content:
This

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day

, we have an opportunity to reflect on something remarkable. 


Across Victoria, our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are growing up in one of the most significant political moments since colonisation. They are the first generation of children to grow up in

Victoria’s Treaty era

. Treaty is about far more than legal agreements or institutional reform. At its heart, Treaty is about people, and most importantly, our children, and our future generations. 


The true measure of any Treaty will not be found in the number of agreements reached or milestones achieved. It will be measured by whether it truly improves the lives of future generations. 


Will Aboriginal children grow up healthier? Will their identity and Connection to their Culture be strong? Will they have every opportunity to learn, thrive and lead? Will they inherit systems that recognise their strengths rather than focus on their disadvantage? 


These are the questions that really matter. 


Aboriginal children already possess extraordinary strengths. They inherit the oldest continuing culture on Earth. They are surrounded by families, Elders and Communities who pass on knowledge, stories and traditions – keeping them strong and keeping them connected to who they are. 


But despite their strengths, many Aboriginal children continue to experience inequitable outcomes across

health

, education,

incarceration

, and wellbeing. Too often, systems have been designed to exclude Aboriginal people and their families, rather than include them.  


Treaty is our chance to change this.  


Treaty allows us to shift decision-making closer to Aboriginal communities, strengthening self-determination and creating services that better reflect the aspirations, cultures and needs of Aboriginal children and families. 


This is not simply about changing policies. It is about changing possibilities. 


Imagine growing up as an Aboriginal child.

Imagine instead of growing up in a State that perpetuates stigma, stereotypes and wants to dismiss your culture in dark history books – you grow up knowing who you are, where you belong and actually understanding your Country and Culture.  


Children have the potential to grow up in a state where their Culture is not only respected but embedded throughout education, healthcare and public life.  Our collective history recognised, our languages celebrated and Community empowered to shape the services that support our families. 


Imagine knowing that decisions about your future are increasingly made by your own people, your Community.

That is the promise that Treaty represents. 


For today’s Aboriginal children, this is not some distant vision. It is unfolding right now, during their own childhood. 


They are the first generation who will remember Victoria before Treaty, and who will one day tell their own children what it was like to witness this historic transformation. 


That is both exciting and humbling, but it also places an extraordinary responsibility on all of us. 


Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day reminds us that children are not just our future leaders – they are citizens of today. Their experiences matter. Their ideas matter. Their voices matter. 


If Treaty is truly about creating a better future, then Aboriginal children must remain at the centre of every conversation. 


Because when today’s children become tomorrow’s Elders, they will not judge this generation by the complexity of negotiations or the wording of agreements. 


They will judge us by outcomes. 


Did we create a Victoria where Aboriginal children could grow up proud of who they are? Did we ensure they remained connected to Culture, Country and Community?  Did we reduce the inequities they inherited? Did we create opportunities for every Aboriginal child and their family to flourish and thrive? 


The answers to those questions will be the enduring measure of success. 


So, this Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children’s Day, let us recognise that our children are growing up during a defining chapter in our state’s history, and work together to ensure it’s done right.


We all must take pride in being the first Australian state to take this historic step and ensure that Treaty is not repealed after the state election. 


Because Treaty is a promise to our future generations.  


A promise that they are not simply growing up in the era of Treaty …

title: High school, university students walk out of class to protest Hanson’s bigotry
content:
High school, university students walk out of class to protest Hanson’s bigotry


Isaac Nellist


Thu, 13/08/2026 - 19:08


Isaac Nellist


August 13, 2026

,


Issue 1460

,


News


Thousands of students joined protests across the country opposing the racism and bigotry of Pauline Hanson and One Nation on August 13. 


See also


Reject One Nation’s call to return to White Australia Policy


How fossil fuel companies target children with climate disinformation


Domestic violence isn’t a ‘two-way street’ and Hanson isn’t confused


The protests were called by the National Union of Students and buoyed by a big turn out of high school students, who skipped school classes to attend the rally. 


The impressive turnout, particularly of high school students, reflects the anger among many young people that Hanson’s far-right politics are getting a hearing in the corporate media, and in-turn being reflected in high polling figures across the country. 


While One Nation has been consistently polling between 25-30%, its support among “Gen Z”, 14–29-year-olds, is around 10%. 


Thousands of students joined the protest in Gadigal Country/Sydney. Photo: Zebedee Parkes


The rally in Gadigal Country/Sydney was electric, with big groups of students arriving with homemade placards, often still wearing their school uniforms. 


University students rallied on campuses across the city before converging on Sydney Town Hall. Students from the University of Sydney briefly took over Redfern Station with chants of “Whose station? Our station!” before catching the train across to Town Hall. 


While many students travelled from nearby inner-city high schools, others travelled from as far as the Blue Mountains, Central Coast and even regional New South Wales to join the rally. 


Students were eager to show their opposition to Hanson's racism. Photo: Peter Boyle


About 2000 students and supporters filled the Town Hall Square, where they heard speeches from student activists and NSW Greens MP Jenny Leong.


References to Hanson, Barnaby Joyce and billionaire Gina Rinehart were met with boos, while calls against racism, transphobia and misogyny were loudly cheered. One student commented that it “felt like a music festival” because of the outpouring of energy and enthusiasm from the youth. 


While anti-racism and opposition to Hanson’s “monoculture” was a key theme, many young people also held signs supporting LGBTIQ rights. 


Protesters then marched around the block before returning to Town Hall Square for a final rally.


A high school student addresses the Gadigal Country/Sydney rally. Photo: Zebedee Parkes


Some of the students who joined the Boorloo/Perth protest. Photo: Petrina Harley


About 1000 high school students from dozens of schools joined the rally in Boorloo/Perth, reports

Blair Vidak

. 


The crowd was large and lively, with many students bringing creative and humorous homemade placards.


They chanted "Unite to fight the right" and "racists not welcome here" as they marched.

author: Nick Reich
title: Introducing the conveners of the Australian Socialist Party: Omar Hassan and Rebecca Barrigos
content:
Over the weekend of 18 July, the Australian Socialist Party was founded. Fledgling as it is, we set ourselves the task of ending an increasingly harsh capitalist system and defeating all the parties who defend that system, from One Nation to the ALP. Achieving that will involve recruiting thousands of socialists to the party, and developing them into activists who can channel the rage of working people into a real force that can win against the odds. 

The Socialist Party’s orientation to its members is unlike any other on the Australian political landscape, where party leaders generally see their members as how-to-vote distribution machines or empty numbers in a faction fight. Socialists aren’t just cheerleaders for parliamentary leaders—our members are fighters. So to help build an active party membership, the Socialist Party founding conference elected two national conveners: Rebecca Barrigos and Omar Hassan.

Both Barrigos and Hassan are teachers and union activists, both have been members of Socialist Alternative since the mid-2000s, both have led impressive campaigns in their home states over the past 20 years, and they’ve each played leading roles in establishing Queensland Socialists and Victorian Socialists respectively. 

Speaking to

Red Flag

, Barrigos remembered the issues that spurred her to join the socialist movement as a uni student:

“The barbarism of the ‘war on terror’, the mass death toll and carnage that was unleashed on the civilian populations of Afghanistan and Iraq, the disgraceful rise of Islamophobia, racism used to justify war crimes, and attacks on civil liberties in the West to quell anti-war opposition, convinced me that I needed to join a socialist organisation that was committed to fighting every institution of the capitalist state.”

Similarly, Hassan related that he “became a socialist in the dark days of the John Howard years, furious at the racism and war that characterised that era”. 

With the resurgence of Hanson’s One Nation and the genocidal wars grinding on in the Middle East, there’s a familiarity to the rage which drove Barrigos and Hassan towards socialism in their youth. The more things change, the more they stay the same.

Sticking it out as socialist activists for two decades, in often difficult circumstances, is an admirable achievement in its own right, but those years meant more than just stubborn principles and passing time for Barrigos and Hassan. They’ve drawn lessons and inspiration from their years of organising. Hassan said that his time on the left has taught him “to appreciate the moments where working-class people come together to fight and win against the system: be it on a small picket line in suburban Melbourne or in mass protests against genocide and imperialism”. 

But mass movements have risen and declined, ebbed and flowed, sometimes scoring small victories but often leaving the fundamental injustice in place. The transience of moments when workers feel their power taught Hassan “how important it is to build a political organisation that can sustain and consolidate the lessons and experiences of those times to build a force that can translate momentum into actual victories”. 

Barrigos made a similar point when speaking about the movement against the Iraq War: “The Iraq War provoked unprecedented resistance. Millions around the world, in Europe, and here in Australia took to the streets in mobilisations even larger than the anti-Vietnam War moratoriums of the 1970s. But despite the size of these rallies, mass protests were never on their own going to stop the US war machine. If we want to win decisively, we need to build a socialist movement that mobilises the power of workers to successfully resist capitalism, and in that fight, lay the basis for a whole different society based on human need, not profit”.

Through their failures and limitations, movements of the past can give their participants a deeper understanding of what’s necessary to win. Not just a firmer conviction, but the right set of politics. Barrigos and Hassan are two among hundreds of experienced socialists who act as conveyor belts for these lessons to a new generation of radicalising young people. There are a few ways they have already been playing this role. They’ve both written insightful theoretical articles for the

Marxist Left Review

 on topics like higher education, the Middle East and Australian politics. They both give impressive speeches.

title: Lami Özgen: Workers should defend common rights and a common future
content:
Former KESK chair Lami Özgen spoke to our agency about the process of democratic integration. Özgen stressed the importance of democratic integration given that the Kurdish people are seeking both to maintain their existence with their own identity and social structure and to live together with Turkish society.


Özgen said: “When we discuss the content of democratic integration, everyone puts forward a particular position and approach according to their political perspective. But what does democratic integration mean for the Kurds as a people, a nation and a society? On the other hand, since the Kurds live together with Turkish society, what does this process mean for Turkish society? In our view, these two questions must be addressed as inseparably connected.”


‘For the first time Kurdish existence has been recognized’


Lami Özgen noted that, after a century of denial, the existence of the Kurdish people has for the first time been recognized through the Peace and Democratic Society Process. He said: “For a hundred years, the Kurdish people have been denied recognition as a nation and a people, and their rights have been usurped. The Kurdish people have always resisted and rebelled against this policy of denial. The Turkish state, with the support of international powers, continued its attacks and carried out massacres. Therefore, in this Peace and Democratic Society Process, which is being pursued for the first time, the existence of the Kurdish people has been recognized.


But a people whose existence is recognized naturally also has rights: national, political and social rights. How will these political, legal and cultural rights be made a reality? How will the dynamics and activists of Kurdish society, from politicians to cultural workers and workers, become integrated into this process?”


‘A legal framework is necessary’


Emphasizing the importance of legal reforms for building a common future with Turkish society, Özgen said: “First and foremost, a solid legal framework is necessary. Once this legal foundation is established, Kurdish society will be able to openly and freely exercise its rights, rebuild its life and future through democratic means and methods within its own society, and at the same time meet Turkish society in a common future.”


‘Democratic integration is not only for political actors’


Özgen added that democratic integration is not limited to political actors and activists. “It is for women, for young people, for workers and for all oppressed sections of society. Recognizing the existence and legal rights of oppressed social groups will come to the fore through democratic methods in this process and take root at the grassroots level,” he said.


‘The struggle of workers was also criminalized because of the war’


Pointing out that the struggle for workers’ rights was also criminalized because of the repressive approach toward the Kurdish struggle, Özgen said: “Undoubtedly, labor forces and workers’ movements play a key role in this period. It can be said that life is built by the hands of workers and laborers. These groups are fundamental social forces and therefore have their own rights and demands. In addition to their political rights, they have legal demands relating to working life.


“However, because of the denial of the Kurds and the ongoing war, these fundamental rights have been trampled on for years, while those fighting for their rights have been criminalized and accused. As a result of this approach by the ruling powers, the struggle of workers has been suppressed and they have been treated negatively.”


Özgen recalled that in Turkey, regulations concerning the labor and employment rights arising from international agreements have not been recognized because of the denial of the Kurds and the ongoing war. He said: “While workers’ rights to organize and their employment rights arising from international conventions have been constitutionally guaranteed in many countries, these rights have not been recognized in Turkey because of the denial of the Kurds and the existing conditions of war; relevant international agreements have either not been signed or have not been put into force.”

title: Tarım işçilerinde asırlık güvencesizlik: 40 derecede 11 saat, 1250 TL
content:
Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Adana - Mevsimlik tarım işçilerinin sayısına ilişkin güncel ve kapsamlı bir resmi veri bulunmazken bu rakamın en az 3 milyonu bulduğu ifade ediliyor. Bu büyük işçi kitlesinin bir parçası da her yıl Urfa’dan Çukurova’ya gelen aileler oluyor. Adana’nın güneyinde, Tuzla yolu üzerindeki Kadıköy civarında bir biber tarlasında karşılaştığımız işçilerin anlattıkları, mevsimlik tarım işçiliğinin değişmeyen tablosunu gösteriyor; düşük yevmiye, uzun çalışma saatleri, kavurucu sıcak, çadırlarda yaşam, aracılara bağımlı sosyal güvencesiz çalışma biçimi ve çocukların eğitimle çalışma arasında bırakılması...

Tuzla yolu üzerindeki Kadıköy civarında bulunan bir biber tarlasında Urfa’dan gelen tarım işçileri aileleriyle birlikte günün büyük bölümünü yüksek sıcaklık ve nem altında çalışarak geçiriyor. Hissedilen sıcaklığın 40 dereceyi aştığı tarlada çalışma günü sabah erken saatlerde başlıyor ve akşama kadar sürüyor. İşçilerin günlük yevmiyesi, elci payı çıkarıldıktan sonra yaklaşık 1250 lira. Kazandıkları para temel ihtiyaçlarını karşılamaya ancak yetiyor. Geçimlerini sağlamak için yevmiyenin en az 2 bin lira olmasını istiyorlar.

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Çoğu çocuklardan oluşan işçilerin bir bölümü biberleri topluyor, bir bölümü sepetlerle taşıyor, bir bölümü de biberleri kasalara diziyor, daha sonra kamyonlara yükleniyor. 25 yaşındaki Merve, biberleri kasalara dizen ekipte. Bir yandan çalışırken bir yandan konuşuyoruz. Adana’ya 15 yıl önce mevsimlik işçi olarak gelmişler ve bir daha Urfa’ya dönmemişler. Tuzla yolu üzerinde kurulu çadırların birinde yaşıyor.

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Merve, çalışma günlerinin sabah saat 06.00’da başladığını, kahvaltının saat 09.00 civarında yapıldığını ve ardından öğlene kadar çalışmaya devam ettiklerini söylüyor. Öğle yemeğinin ardından yeniden tarlaya döndüklerini belirten Merve, işin saat 17.00’ye kadar sürdüğünü ifade ediyor. Yüksek sıcaklığın çalışma koşullarını daha da ağırlaştırdığını söyleyen Merve, “Çok sıcak, çok zor bizim için. Çadırlarda yaşıyoruz. 1250 TL alıyoruz, bir şey getirmiyor. Yani rezillik içindeyiz” diyor. Merve, Urfa’da kendilerine ait bir evlerinin olduğunu ancak ailenin ekonomik durumunun yeni bir ev yapmaya ya da yaşam koşullarını iyileştirmeye yetmediğini anlatıyor. Tarım işçiliğinden elde ettikleri gelirin önemli bölümünün gıda ve temel ihtiyaçlara gittiğini, birikim yapamadıklarını söyleyen Merve en az 2 bin lira yevmiye ve sigorta taleplerini dile getiriyor.

Tarladaki çalışma yalnızca gün boyunca yapılan tarım işinden ibaret değil. Merve anlatıyor: “Akşama çadıra geçiyoruz. Eve gittiğimizde dinlenemiyoruz. İş olur, çadır işi, çamaşır, bulaşık yıkıyoruz.”

Urfa’dan gelen ve aynı tarlada çalışanlardan biri de 13 yaşındaki Emine Özlem. Okulu 6. sınıfta bırakmış. Okulu bırakma nedenini ise kısa ve doğrudan ifade ediyor: “İş yüzünden.”

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Emine, daha önce okula giderken derslerinin iyi olduğunu söylüyor. Eğitimine devam etmek konusunda ise bir “İstiyorum” diyor, sonra düşünüp “İstemiyorum…” diyor. “Ne olmak isterdin?” sorusuna ise “Doktor olmak isterdim” diye cevap veriyor.

Bir diğer çocuk işçi ise 14 yaşındaki Güneş. Güneş okulu bırakmamış, 8. sınıfa geçmiş, ancak kendisini okutmak için çalışan çocuklardan. Bu yıl ilk kez tarlada çalışmaya gelmiş.

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Heyecandan kısa kısa cevap veriyor;

- “Ailem gelmek istedi, onun için geldim.”

- “Geleceğim için, okumak için”

Urfa’ya döndüğünde kazandığı parayı okul ihtiyaçları için kullanacağını anlatıyor. Test kitapları ve diğer eğitim ihtiyaçlarını almak istediğini söylüyor. “Bir de hakim olmak istiyorum. Gittiğimde çabalayıp okuyacağım. Okul için testler alacağım. İhtiyaçlarımı alacağım. Onun için…”

Güneş’in ailesinden beş kişi birlikte çalışıyor. Yaklaşık 12 saatlerini tarlada geçiriyorlar. Sabah 06.00-06.30 civarında geliyorlar ve eve çok geç dönüyorlar. Çalışmanın kendisi için “çok yorucu” olduğunu söyleyen Güneş, “Adaletsizlik.” diyor. Günlük ücretin 2 bin TL civarında olmasını istiyor, nedenini de “Çünkü çok çalışıyoruz” sözleriyle açıklıyor.
